declarations.docstring:
**Erdős Problem 329.**
Let `A ⊆ ℕ` be a Sidon set. How large can
`lim sup_{N → ∞} |A ∩ {1,…,N}| / N^{1/2}`
be?
references: [erdosproblems.com/329](https://www.erdosproblems.com/329)
[AlMi25] B. Alexeev and D. G. Mixon, Forbidden Sidon subsets of perfect difference sets, featuring a human-assisted proof. [arXiv:2510.19804](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.19804) (2025).
[Ha47] Hall, Jr., Marshall, Cyclic projective planes. Duke Math. J. (1947), 1079--1090.
declarations.type_pretty: sSup {x | ∃ A, ∃ (_ : IsSidon A), Erdos329.sidonUpperDensity A = x} = Erdos329.erdos_329.answer

declarations.docstring:
The converse: if the maximum density is 1, then any finite Sidon set
can be embedded in a perfect difference set modulo $n > 0$.

Since the consequent is false (due to the counterexamples in [Ha47] and [AlMi25]),
this implication is logically equivalent to the statement that the maximum upper
density of Sidon sets is NOT 1.
Because the maximum upper density problem is still open, the truth value of this
implication is also an open research problem.
references: [erdosproblems.com/329](https://www.erdosproblems.com/329)
[AlMi25] B. Alexeev and D. G. Mixon, Forbidden Sidon subsets of perfect difference sets, featuring a human-assisted proof. [arXiv:2510.19804](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.19804) (2025).
[Ha47] Hall, Jr., Marshall, Cyclic projective planes. Duke Math. J. (1947), 1079--1090.
declarations.type_pretty:
sSup {x | ∃ A, ∃ (_ : IsSidon A), Erdos329.sidonUpperDensity A = x} = 1 →
  ∀ (A : Finset ℕ), IsSidon ↑A → ∃ D n, ∃ (_ : n > 0), ↑A ⊆ D ∧ IsPerfectDifferenceSet D n

declarations.docstring:
Krückeberg ([Kr61]) exhibited an infinite Sidon set `A` with
`sidonUpperDensity A = 1 / Real.sqrt 2`, improving Erdős’ earlier
`1 / 2` lower bound.

[Kr61] Krückeberg, Fritz, $B\sb{2}$-Folgen und verwandte Zahlenfolgen. J. Reine Angew. Math. (1961), 53-60.
references: [erdosproblems.com/329](https://www.erdosproblems.com/329)
[AlMi25] B. Alexeev and D. G. Mixon, Forbidden Sidon subsets of perfect difference sets, featuring a human-assisted proof. [arXiv:2510.19804](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.19804) (2025).
[Ha47] Hall, Jr., Marshall, Cyclic projective planes. Duke Math. J. (1947), 1079--1090.
declarations.type_pretty: ∃ A, IsSidon A ∧ Erdos329.sidonUpperDensity A = 1 / √2

declarations.docstring:
Erdős proved that upper density `1 / 2` can be attained; in particular,
there exists a Sidon set whose upper density is *at least* `1 / 2`.
references: [erdosproblems.com/329](https://www.erdosproblems.com/329)
[AlMi25] B. Alexeev and D. G. Mixon, Forbidden Sidon subsets of perfect difference sets, featuring a human-assisted proof. [arXiv:2510.19804](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.19804) (2025).
[Ha47] Hall, Jr., Marshall, Cyclic projective planes. Duke Math. J. (1947), 1079--1090.
declarations.type_pretty: ∃ A, IsSidon A ∧ Erdos329.sidonUpperDensity A ≥ 1 / 2

declarations.docstring:
Erdős and Turán [ErTu41] proved the upper bound of 1.

[ErTu41] Erdős, P. and Turán, P., On a problem of Sidon in additive number theory, and on some related problems. J. London Math. Soc. (1941), 212-215.
references: [erdosproblems.com/329](https://www.erdosproblems.com/329)
[AlMi25] B. Alexeev and D. G. Mixon, Forbidden Sidon subsets of perfect difference sets, featuring a human-assisted proof. [arXiv:2510.19804](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.19804) (2025).
[Ha47] Hall, Jr., Marshall, Cyclic projective planes. Duke Math. J. (1947), 1079--1090.
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (A : Set ℕ), IsSidon A → Erdos329.sidonUpperDensity A ≤ 1

declarations.docstring: It is possible to construct a Sidon set with positive density.
references: [erdosproblems.com/329](https://www.erdosproblems.com/329)
[AlMi25] B. Alexeev and D. G. Mixon, Forbidden Sidon subsets of perfect difference sets, featuring a human-assisted proof. [arXiv:2510.19804](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.19804) (2025).
[Ha47] Hall, Jr., Marshall, Cyclic projective planes. Duke Math. J. (1947), 1079--1090.
declarations.type_pretty: ∃ A, IsSidon A ∧ 0 < Erdos329.sidonUpperDensity A

declarations.docstring:
Let `A ⊆ ℕ` be a set such that every integer can be written as `n^2 + a`
for some `a` in `A` and `n ≥ 0`. What is the smallest possible value of
`lim sup n → ∞ |A ∩ {1, …, N}| / N^(1/2)`?
references: [erdosproblems.com/33](https://www.erdosproblems.com/33)
declarations.type_pretty: ⨅ A, Filter.limsup (fun N => ↑(↑A ∩ Set.Icc 1 N).ncard / ↑√↑N) Filter.atTop = Erdos33.erdos_33.answer

declarations.docstring:
Erdos observed that this value is finite and > 1. This records the lower bound `> 1`,
i.e. that `1` is a strict lower bound for every admissible `A`; the finiteness is
`erdos_33.variants.vanDoorn`.
references: [erdosproblems.com/33](https://www.erdosproblems.com/33)
declarations.type_pretty: 1 < ⨅ A, Filter.limsup (fun N => ↑(↑A ∩ Set.Icc 1 N).ncard / ↑√↑N) Filter.atTop

declarations.docstring:
The smallest possible value of `lim sup n → ∞ |A ∩ {1, …, N}| / N^(1/2)`
is at most `2φ^(5/2) ≈ 6.66`, with `φ` equal to the golden ratio. Proven by
Wouter van Doorn.
references: [erdosproblems.com/33](https://www.erdosproblems.com/33)
declarations.type_pretty: ⨅ A, Filter.limsup (fun N => ↑(↑A ∩ Set.Icc 1 N).ncard / ↑√↑N) Filter.atTop ≤ ↑(2 * Real.goldenRatio ^ (5 / 2))

declarations.docstring:
Let $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ and $D(A)$ be the set of those numbers which occur infinitely often as
$a_1 - a_2$ with $a_1, a_2\in A$. What conditions on $A$ are sufficient to ensure $D(A)$ has bounded
gaps?

The sufficient conditions are the unknown `erdos_332.answer`. In order to solve this problem one
has to provide what the sufficient conditions are, and proof that they imply the desired condition.
If the condition is a solution to the problem is up to human judgement.
references: [erdosproblems.com/332](https://www.erdosproblems.com/332)
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (A : Set ℕ), Erdos332.erdos_332.answer A → Erdos332.HasBoundedGaps (Erdos332.D_A A)

declarations.docstring:
The restricted order of a basis $A$ is the least integer $t$ (if it exists) such that every large
integer is the sum of at most $t$ distinct summands from $A$. What are necessary and sufficient
conditions that this exists?

A solution must fill in `Erdos338.erdos_338.answer` with the condition and prove the
equivalence. Whether a condition is a satisfactory answer is up to human judgement.
references: [erdosproblems.com/338](https://www.erdosproblems.com/338)

declarations.docstring:
Can the restricted order of a basis be bounded (when it exists) in terms of the order of the
basis?

`HasOrder A h` only says that the order of $A$ is at most $h$. This gives the same question,
since $f$ can be replaced by its running maximum. Kelly [Ke57] showed that $f(2) = 4$ works, and
Hennecart [He05] showed that $4$ is optimal. Hegyvári, Hennecart and Plagne [HHP07] showed that
any such $f$ has $f(k) \geq 2^{k-2}+k-1$ for $k \geq 3$.
references: [erdosproblems.com/338](https://www.erdosproblems.com/338)
[ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
[ErGr80b] Erdős, P. and Graham, R. L., *On bases with an exact order*. Acta Arith. (1980), 201-207.
[HHP07] Hegyvári, Norbert and Hennecart, François and Plagne, Alain, *Answer to a question by Burr and Erdős on restricted addition, and related results*. Combin. Probab. Comput. (2007), 747--756.
[He05] Hennecart, François, *On the restricted order of asymptotic bases of order two*. Ramanujan J. (2005), 123--130.
[Ke57] Kelly, John B., *Restricted bases*. Amer. J. Math. (1957), 258-264.
[Pa33] Pall, Gordon, *On Sums of Squares*. Amer. Math. Monthly (1933), 10-18.
[Sc54] Schinzel, A., *Sur la décomposition des nombres naturels en sommes de nombres triangulaires distincts*. Bull. Acad. Polon. Sci. Cl. III. (1954), 409-410.
declarations.type_pretty:
∃ f,
  ∀ (A : Set ℕ) (h : ℕ),
    Erdos338.HasOrder A h → (∃ t, Erdos338.HasRestrictedOrder A t) → Erdos338.HasRestrictedOrder A (f h)

declarations.docstring:
What are necessary and sufficient conditions that the restricted order of a basis $A$ is equal to
the order of $A$?

For a basis, `basisOrder A` is finite, so the equality also says that the restricted order exists.
The condition is `Erdos338.erdos_338.variants.eq_order.answer`, as in `Erdos338.erdos_338`.
references: [erdosproblems.com/338](https://www.erdosproblems.com/338)
[ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
[ErGr80b] Erdős, P. and Graham, R. L., *On bases with an exact order*. Acta Arith. (1980), 201-207.
[HHP07] Hegyvári, Norbert and Hennecart, François and Plagne, Alain, *Answer to a question by Burr and Erdős on restricted addition, and related results*. Combin. Probab. Comput. (2007), 747--756.
[He05] Hennecart, François, *On the restricted order of asymptotic bases of order two*. Ramanujan J. (2005), 123--130.

[Pa33] Pall, Gordon, *On Sums of Squares*. Amer. Math. Monthly (1933), 10-18.
[Sc54] Schinzel, A., *Sur la décomposition des nombres naturels en sommes de nombres triangulaires distincts*. Bull. Acad. Polon. Sci. Cl. III. (1954), 409-410.

∀ (A : Set ℕ),
  (∃ h, Erdos338.HasOrder A h) →
    (Erdos338.restrictedOrder A = Erdos338.basisOrder A ↔ Erdos338.erdos_338.variants.eq_order.answer A)

declarations.docstring:
Hegyvári, Hennecart and Plagne [HHP07] showed that for all $k \geq 2$ there exists a basis of
order $k$ which has restricted order at least $2^{k-2}+k-1$.

The basis built in the proof of Theorem 4 of [HHP07] (for $k \geq 3$) has order exactly $k$ and a
finite restricted order, equal to $2^{k-2}+k-1$. The finiteness matters: without it, Bateman's
example `Erdos338.erdos_338.variants.bateman` would already give the bound. For $k = 2$ the bound
is $2$, and $A = \{1\} \cup \{x : 2 \mid x\}$ works.
references: [erdosproblems.com/338](https://www.erdosproblems.com/338)
[ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
[ErGr80b] Erdős, P. and Graham, R. L., *On bases with an exact order*. Acta Arith. (1980), 201-207.
[HHP07] Hegyvári, Norbert and Hennecart, François and Plagne, Alain, *Answer to a question by Burr and Erdős on restricted addition, and related results*. Combin. Probab. Comput. (2007), 747--756.
[He05] Hennecart, François, *On the restricted order of asymptotic bases of order two*. Ramanujan J. (2005), 123--130.
[Ke57] Kelly, John B., *Restricted bases*. Amer. J. Math. (1957), 258-264.
[Pa33] Pall, Gordon, *On Sums of Squares*. Amer. Math. Monthly (1933), 10-18.
[Sc54] Schinzel, A., *Sur la décomposition des nombres naturels en sommes de nombres triangulaires distincts*. Bull. Acad. Polon. Sci. Cl. III. (1954), 409-410.
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (k : ℕ), 2 ≤ k → ∃ A, Erdos338.basisOrder A = ↑k ∧ Erdos338.restrictedOrder A = ↑(2 ^ (k - 2) + k - 1)

declarations.docstring:
Is it true that if the sets $A \setminus F$, for all finite sets $F$, are bases of the same order,
then $A$ must have a restricted order?

We read "the same order" literally: every $A \setminus F$ has the same exact order $h$. This is
equivalent to asking that the orders of the sets $A \setminus F$ are bounded. Removing elements can
only raise the order, so if the orders are bounded, their maximum is attained at some $F_0$, and
$A \setminus F_0 \subseteq A$ satisfies the literal hypothesis.
references: [erdosproblems.com/338](https://www.erdosproblems.com/338)
[ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).

[Sc54] Schinzel, A., *Sur la décomposition des nombres naturels en sommes de nombres triangulaires distincts*. Bull. Acad. Polon. Sci. Cl. III. (1954), 409-410.

declarations.docstring:
The set of squares has order $4$ and restricted order $5$ (see [Pa33]).

Here $0$ is a square. The order is $4$ by Lagrange's four-square theorem, and is not $3$ because
no integer $\equiv 7 \pmod 8$ is a sum of three squares.

declarations.docstring:

declarations.docstring:
If $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is a set of integers such that
$$\lvert A\cap \{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert\gg N^{1/2}$$
for all $N$ then must $A$ be subcomplete? That is, must
$$P(A) = \left\{\sum_{n\in B}n : B\subseteq A\textrm{ finite }\right\}$$
contain an infinite arithmetic progression?

This is true, and was proved by Szemerédi and Vu [SzVu06].

The implied constant is absolute, as in [SzVu06b, Corollary 1.4].
references: [erdosproblems.com/344](https://www.erdosproblems.com/344)
[ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
[Er61b] Erdős, P., *On the representation of large integers as sums of distinct summands taken from a fixed set*. Acta Arith. (1961/62), 345-354.
[Fo66] Folkman, J., *On the representation of integers as sums of distinct terms from a fixed sequence*. Canadian J. Math. 18 (1966), 643-655.
[SzVu06] Szemerédi, E. and Vu, V., *Long arithmetic progressions in sumsets: thresholds and bounds*. J. Amer. Math. Soc. 19 (2006), 119-169.
[SzVu06b] Szemerédi, E. and Vu, V., *Finite and infinite arithmetic progressions in sumsets*. Ann. of Math. 163 (2006), 1-35.
declarations.type_pretty: ∃ C, 0 < C ∧ ∀ (A : Set ℕ), (∀ᶠ (N : ℕ) in Filter.atTop, C * √↑N ≤ ↑(A.countUpTo N)) → IsSubcomplete A

declarations.docstring:
Let $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be a complete sequence, and define the threshold of completeness
$T(A)$ to be the least integer $m$ such that all $n\geq m$ are in
$$P(A) = \left\{\sum_{n\in B}n : B\subseteq A\textrm{ finite }\right\}$$
(the existence of $T(A)$ is guaranteed by completeness).

Is it true that there are infinitely many $k$ such that $T(n^k)>T(n^{k+1})$?

Here $T(n^k)$ means the threshold of the positive $k$-th powers. Least-threshold witnesses
ensure that the thresholds exist. We restrict to $k\geq 1$, since the zeroth powers form
$\{1\}$, which is incomplete. Positive powers are complete [Ki17].
references: [erdosproblems.com/345](https://www.erdosproblems.com/345)
[ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980), p. 55.

[Ki17] Kim, D., *On the largest integer that is not a sum of distinct positive nth powers*. Journal of Integer Sequences 20 (2017), Article 17.7.5. [arXiv:1610.02439](https://arxiv.org/abs/1610.02439)
declarations.type_pretty:
{k |
    0 < k ∧
      ∃ a b,
        IsLeast (IsAddComplete.thresholds (Erdos345.kthPowers k)) a ∧
          IsLeast (IsAddComplete.thresholds (Erdos345.kthPowers (k + 1))) b ∧ b < a}.Infinite

declarations.docstring:
For $\alpha > 2$ and any $t > 0$, the sequence $\lfloor t\alpha^n\rfloor$ is not additively
complete; equivalently $(t, \alpha)$ is not a "good pair". A partial result on the open Erdős
Problem 349: it complements `complete_for_alpha_in_Ioo_one_to_goldenRatio`.

The proof is recorded via the `formal_proof` mechanism rather than written inline, as it exceeds
the repository's proof-length guideline.
references: [erdosproblems.com/349](https://www.erdosproblems.com/349)
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (t α : ℝ), 0 < t → 2 < α → ¬Erdos349.IsGoodPair t α

declarations.docstring:
For $0 < \alpha \le 1$ and any $t > 0$, $(t, \alpha)$ is not a good pair: every term
$\lfloor t\alpha^n\rfloor$ lies in the finite interval $[0, \lfloor t\rfloor]$ (since
$\alpha^n \le 1$), so every subset sum is bounded by the constant $\sum_{i \in [0,\lfloor t\rfloor]} i$,
and no large integer can be a subset sum. A partial result on the open Erdős Problem 349,
complementing the $2 < \alpha$ and integer-coefficient cases.
references: [erdosproblems.com/349](https://www.erdosproblems.com/349)
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (t α : ℝ), 0 < t → 0 < α → α ≤ 1 → ¬Erdos349.IsGoodPair t α

It seems likely that the sequence is complete for all
for all $t>0$ and all $1 < \alpha < \frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}$.
references: [erdosproblems.com/349](https://www.erdosproblems.com/349)

declarations.docstring:
**The dyadic fiber at $\alpha = 2$.** For every $k$, the pair $(1/2^k, 2)$ is good: the
sequence $\lfloor 2^n / 2^k\rfloor$ is additively complete because at index $n = m + k$ it equals
the exact power $2^m$, so its range contains all powers of two, which already form an additively
complete set. Uses monotonicity `IsAddComplete.mono`.
references: [erdosproblems.com/349](https://www.erdosproblems.com/349)
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (k : ℕ), Erdos349.IsGoodPair (1 / 2 ^ k) 2

(that is, all sufficiently large integers are the sum of distinct integers of the form $\lfloor t\alpha^n\rfloor$)?

declarations.docstring:
**Binary expansion.** Every natural number $k$ is a sum of distinct powers of two: there is
a finite set $E$ of exponents with $k = \sum_{i \in E} 2^i$. Proved by strong induction:
subtract the largest power $2^m \le k$, recurse on the remainder. A textbook-level building
block for `one_two_isGoodPair` below; it says nothing about `IsGoodPair` itself.
references: [erdosproblems.com/349](https://www.erdosproblems.com/349)

declarations.docstring:
For any $k$ there exists some $t_k\in (0,1)$ such that the set of $\alpha > 0$
such that the sequence $\lfloor t_k\alpha^n\rfloor$ is complete consists of at least $k$
disjoint line segments, that is, it has at least $k$ connected components.
references: [erdosproblems.com/349](https://www.erdosproblems.com/349)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (k : ℕ),
  ∃ t ∈ Set.Ioo 0 1,
    have S := {α | 0 < α ∧ Erdos349.IsGoodPair t α};
    ↑k ≤ (connectedComponentIn S '' S).encard

declarations.docstring:
**Integer leading coefficient $t \ge 2$ blocks completeness.** For every integer base
$\alpha$, the pair $(t, \alpha)$ with integer $t \ge 2$ is not good: $\lfloor t\alpha^n\rfloor =
t\alpha^n$ is a multiple of $t$, so every subset sum is too, but two consecutive large integers
cannot both be multiples of $t$. Generalizes the parity obstruction ($t = 2$). A partial result
on Erdős Problem 349.
references: [erdosproblems.com/349](https://www.erdosproblems.com/349)
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (t : ℤ), 2 ≤ t → ∀ (α : ℤ), ¬Erdos349.IsGoodPair ↑t ↑α

declarations.docstring:
**Erdős Problem 349, complete characterization on positive integer pairs.** For integers
$t \ge 1$, $\alpha \ge 1$, the pair $(t, \alpha)$ is good (i.e. $\lfloor t\alpha^n\rfloor$ is
additively complete) iff $(t, \alpha) = (1, 2)$. Assembles the four partial results: $(1,2)$ is
good, $\alpha \le 1$ fails, $2 < \alpha$ fails (`alpha_gt_two_not_isGoodPair`), and integer
$t \ge 2$ fails.
references: [erdosproblems.com/349](https://www.erdosproblems.com/349)
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (t α : ℤ), 1 ≤ t → 1 ≤ α → (Erdos349.IsGoodPair ↑t ↑α ↔ t = 1 ∧ α = 2)

declarations.docstring:
**The pair $(1, 2)$ is good.** The powers of two $\lfloor 1\cdot 2^n\rfloor = 2^n$ form an
additively complete set: every $k \ge 1$ is a finite sum of distinct powers of two.
references: [erdosproblems.com/349](https://www.erdosproblems.com/349)
declarations.type_pretty: Erdos349.IsGoodPair 1 2

declarations.docstring:
**The pair $(3/2, 2)$ is NOT good.** The negative companion of `dyadic_two_isGoodPair`:
while every dyadic coefficient $1/2^k$ gives a good pair at $\alpha = 2$, the non-dyadic rational
$t = 3/2$ does not. The sequence $\lfloor (3/2)\cdot 2^n\rfloor = 1, 3, 6, 12, 24, \ldots$ is not
additively complete because every term but the first $\lfloor 3/2\rfloor = 1$ is a multiple of
$3$ (namely $\lfloor (3/2)\cdot 2^{n+1}\rfloor = 3\cdot 2^n$), so every subset sum is
$\equiv 0$ or $1 \pmod 3$; the infinitely many integers $\equiv 2 \pmod 3$ are never reached.
A partial result on Erdős Problem 349 in the same divisibility family as
`int_coeff_ge_two_not_isGoodPair` (here the modulus is $3$).
references: [erdosproblems.com/349](https://www.erdosproblems.com/349)
declarations.type_pretty: ¬Erdos349.IsGoodPair (3 / 2) 2

declarations.docstring:
Is there some $c > 0$ such that every measurable $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ of measure $\geq c$
contains the vertices of a triangle of area 1?
references: [erdosproblems.com/352](https://www.erdosproblems.com/352)
declarations.type_pretty:
∃ c > 0,
  ∀ (A : Set (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2))),
    MeasurableSet A →
      ↑(MeasureTheory.volume A) ≥ ↑c →

declarations.docstring:
Let $A=\{a_1 < \cdots\}$ be an infinite sequence of integers. Let $f(n)$ count the number of
solutions to $$n=\sum_{u\leq i\leq v}a_i.$$
Is there such an $A$ for which $f(n)\to \infty$ as $n\to \infty$?

Tao [Ta26] constructed such a sequence with $f(n) \gg \log n$ for all sufficiently large $n$.
references: [erdosproblems.com/358](https://www.erdosproblems.com/358)
[Ta26] T. Tao, [Erdős problem 358](https://terrytao.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/erdos-358-2.pdf) (2026)
declarations.type_pretty: ∃ A, StrictMono A ∧ Filter.Tendsto (Erdos358.f A) Filter.atTop Filter.atTop

declarations.docstring:
Let $A=\{a_1 < \cdots\}$ be an infinite sequence of integers. Let $f(n)$ count the number of
solutions to $$n=\sum_{u\leq i\leq v}a_i.$$
Is there an $A$ such that $f(n)\geq 2$ for all large $n$?

This also follows from Tao's construction with $f(n) \gg \log n$ [Ta26].
references: [erdosproblems.com/358](https://www.erdosproblems.com/358)
[Ta26] T. Tao, [Erdős problem 358](https://terrytao.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/erdos-358-2.pdf) (2026)
declarations.type_pretty: ∃ A, StrictMono A ∧ ∀ᶠ (n : ℕ) in Filter.atTop, 2 ≤ Erdos358.f A n

declarations.docstring:
In [ErGr80] Erdős and Graham further asked whether there is an $A$ with $f(n)\geq 1$ for all
large $n$. Egami observed that this holds trivially for $a_n=n$, so they may have intended to
count only those representations $$n=\sum_{u\leq i\leq v}a_i$$ that use at least two consecutive
terms, which is what $g$ counts.

This follows from Tao's construction [Ta26], which gives $f(n)\gg\log n$: see
`erdos_358.parts.ii` and `one_le_g_of_two_le_f`.
references: [erdosproblems.com/358](https://www.erdosproblems.com/358)
[Ta26] T. Tao, [Erdős problem 358](https://terrytao.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/erdos-358-2.pdf) (2026)
declarations.type_pretty: ∃ A, StrictMono A ∧ ∀ᶠ (n : ℕ) in Filter.atTop, 1 ≤ Erdos358.g A n

declarations.docstring:
This example calculates the value of $M 1$. The set is $\{1, 2\}$, so the only partition is
$A = \{1\}, B = \{2\}$ (or vice versa). The possible differences are $1 - 2 = -1$ and $2 - 1 = 1$.
The `Overlap` for $k=-1$ is 1 (if $A=\{1\}, B=\{2\}$) and for $k=1$ also 1 (if $A=\{2\}, B=\{1\}$ ).
The `MaxOverlap` is $1$, since the `Overlap` is $0$ for other $k$.
Thus, $M 1 = 1$.
references: [erdosproblems.com/36](https://www.erdosproblems.com/36)
[Wikipedial: Minimum overlap problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimum_overlap_problem)
declarations.type_pretty: Erdos36.M 1 = 1

declarations.docstring:

has all four pairwise differences ($\pm 1, \pm 2$) distinct, so `MaxOverlap = 1`.
Any balanced partition has both pieces nonempty, so `MaxOverlap \geq 1`.
references: [erdosproblems.com/36](https://www.erdosproblems.com/36)
[Wikipedial: Minimum overlap problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimum_overlap_problem)
declarations.type_pretty: Erdos36.M 2 = 1

declarations.docstring:
Do all pairs of consecutive powerful numbers $n$ and $n+1$ come from solutions to Pell
equations? In other words, must either $n$ or $n+1$ be a square?

The answer to the first question is no: Golomb [Go70] observed that both $12167=23^3$ and
$12168=2^3 3^2 13^2$ are powerful.

We require $n>0$ since `Nat.Powerful` also includes $0$.
references: [erdosproblems.com/365](https://www.erdosproblems.com/365)
[Go70] Golomb, S. W., *Powerful numbers*. Amer. Math. Monthly (1970), 848-855.
[Gu04] Guy, R. K., *Unsolved problems in number theory* (2004), Problem B16.
[Wa76] Walker, D. T., *Consecutive integer pairs of powerful numbers and related Diophantine equations*. Fibonacci Quart. (1976), 111-116.
declarations.type_pretty: ¬∀ (n : ℕ), 0 < n → n.Powerful → (n + 1).Powerful → IsSquare n ∨ IsSquare (n + 1)

    ∃ k, ∀ᶠ (x : ℕ) in Filter.atTop, ↑{n | 0 < n ∧ n ≤ x ∧ n.Powerful ∧ (n + 1).Powerful}.ncard ≤ C * Real.log ↑x ^ k

declarations.docstring:
Let $B_2(n)$ be the $2$-full part of $n$ (that is, $B_2(n)=n/n'$ where $n'$ is the product of all
primes that divide $n$ exactly once). Is it true that, for every fixed $k \geq 1$,
$\prod_{n \leq m < n+k} B_2(m) \ll n^{2+o(1)}$?
references: [erdosproblems.com/367](https://www.erdosproblems.com/367)
[ErGr80] P. Erdős and R. L. Graham, *Old and New Problems and Results in Combinatorial Number Theory*, L'Enseignement Mathématique (1980).
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (k : ℕ),
  1 ≤ k →
    ∃ e,
      e =o[Filter.atTop] 1 ∧ ∀ᶠ (n : ℕ) in Filter.atTop, ↑(∏ m ∈ Finset.Ico n (n + k), Erdos367.B 2 m) ≤ ↑n ^ (2 + e n)

declarations.docstring:
Or perhaps even $\prod_{n \leq m < n+k} B_2(m) \ll_k n^2$?

van Doorn notes in the comments that this fails for all $k \geq 3$.
references: [erdosproblems.com/367](https://www.erdosproblems.com/367)
[ErGr80] P. Erdős and R. L. Graham, *Old and New Problems and Results in Combinatorial Number Theory*, L'Enseignement Mathématique (1980).
declarations.type_pretty: ¬∀ (k : ℕ), 1 ≤ k → (fun n => ↑(∏ m ∈ Finset.Ico n (n + k), Erdos367.B 2 m)) =O[Filter.atTop] fun n => ↑n ^ 2

declarations.docstring:
It would also be interesting to find upper and lower bounds for the analogous product with $B_r$
for $r \geq 3$, where $B_r(n)$ is the $r$-full part of $n$ (that is, the product of prime powers
$p^a \mid n$ such that $p^{a+1} \nmid n$ and $a \geq r$). Is it true that, for every fixed
$r \geq 3$ and $k \geq 2$, there is some $\epsilon = \epsilon(r, k) > 0$ with
$\limsup \frac{\prod_{n \leq m < n+k} B_r(m)}{n^{1+\epsilon}} = \infty$?

The webpage writes "for every fixed $r,k \geq 2$ and $\epsilon > 0$", but van Doorn observes in
the [comments](https://www.erdosproblems.com/forum/thread/367#post-1766) that the intended
reading lets $\epsilon$ depend on $r$ and $k$. Since $B_r(m) \mid m$, the product is at most
$\prod_{n \leq m < n+k} m$, so the reading with $\epsilon$ universally quantified is false.

The answer is yes: $\epsilon = 1/(2r)$ works. For $j \geq r$ let $x = 2^j + 1$ and $n = x^r - 1$;
then $B_r(n+1) = x^r$ and $2^j \mid n$ gives $B_r(n) \geq 2^j$, so the product over $[n, n+k)$ is at
least $2^j x^r \geq (\sqrt{x}/2)\, n^{1 + 1/(2r)}$, which is unbounded. A stronger exponent
(any $\epsilon < (r+1)/r^2$) is claimed in the [forum](https://www.erdosproblems.com/forum/thread/367)
but is not formalised.
references: [erdosproblems.com/367](https://www.erdosproblems.com/367)
[ErGr80] P. Erdős and R. L. Graham, *Old and New Problems and Results in Combinatorial Number Theory*, L'Enseignement Mathématique (1980).
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (r k : ℕ),
  3 ≤ r →
    2 ≤ k →
      ∃ ε,
        0 < ε ∧
          Filter.limsup (fun n => ↑(↑(∏ m ∈ Finset.Ico n (n + k), Erdos367.B r m) / ↑n ^ (1 + ε))) Filter.atTop = ⊤

declarations.docstring:
But this fails for all $k \geq 3$, and in fact
$\prod_{n \leq m < n+3} B_2(m) \gg n^2 \log n$ infinitely often.
references: [erdosproblems.com/367](https://www.erdosproblems.com/367)
[ErGr80] P. Erdős and R. L. Graham, *Old and New Problems and Results in Combinatorial Number Theory*, L'Enseignement Mathématique (1980).
declarations.type_pretty: ∃ c > 0, ∃ᶠ (n : ℕ) in Filter.atTop, c * (↑n ^ 2 * Real.log ↑n) ≤ ↑(∏ m ∈ Finset.Ico n (n + 3), Erdos367.B 2 m)

declarations.docstring:
van Doorn notes in the comments that for $k \leq 2$ we trivially have
$\prod_{n \leq m < n+k} B_2(m) \ll n^2$.
references: [erdosproblems.com/367](https://www.erdosproblems.com/367)
[ErGr80] P. Erdős and R. L. Graham, *Old and New Problems and Results in Combinatorial Number Theory*, L'Enseignement Mathématique (1980).
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ k ≤ 2, (fun n => ↑(∏ m ∈ Finset.Ico n (n + k), Erdos367.B 2 m)) =O[Filter.atTop] fun n => ↑n ^ 2

declarations.docstring:
It is easy to see that for any `n ≥ 1` and `k ≤ 2`, if `n + 1, ..., n + k` are all composite,
then there are distinct primes `p₁, ... pₖ` such that `pᵢ ∣ n + i` for all `1 ≤ i ≤ k`.
references: [erdosproblems.com/375](https://www.erdosproblems.com/375)
[ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
[RST75] Ramachandra, K. and Shorey, T. N. and Tijdeman, R., On Grimm's problem relating to factorisation of a block of consecutive integers. J. Reine Angew. Math. (1975), 109-124. -
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ n ≥ 1,
  ∀ k ≤ 2,
    (∀ i < k, ¬Nat.Prime (n + i + 1)) → ∃ p, Function.Injective p ∧ ∀ (i : Fin k), Nat.Prime (p i) ∧ p i ∣ n + ↑i + 1

declarations.docstring: In particular, if `Erdos375Prop` is true, then Legendre's conjecture is asymptotically true.
references: [erdosproblems.com/375](https://www.erdosproblems.com/375)
[ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
[RST75] Ramachandra, K. and Shorey, T. N. and Tijdeman, R., On Grimm's problem relating to factorisation of a block of consecutive integers. J. Reine Angew. Math. (1975), 109-124. -

declarations.docstring:
There exists a constant `c > 0` such that for all `n`, if
`k < c * (log n / (log (log n))) ^ 3 → (∀ i < k, ¬ (n + i + 1).Prime)`, then
there are distinct primes `p₁, ... pₖ` such that `pᵢ ∣ n + i` for all `1 ≤ i ≤ k`. This is proved
in [RST75]. There is no need to only consider sufficiently large `n` because one can always take
`c` small enough so that `k < c * (log n / (log (log n))) ^ 3` implies that `k = 0` until `n` is
large.
references: [erdosproblems.com/375](https://www.erdosproblems.com/375)
[ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
[RST75] Ramachandra, K. and Shorey, T. N. and Tijdeman, R., On Grimm's problem relating to factorisation of a block of consecutive integers. J. Reine Angew. Math. (1975), 109-124. -
declarations.type_pretty:
∃ c > 0,
  ∀ (n k : ℕ),
    ↑k < c * (Real.log ↑n / Real.log (Real.log ↑n)) ^ 3 →
      (∀ i < k, ¬Nat.Prime (n + i + 1)) → ∃ p, Function.Injective p ∧ ∀ (i : Fin k), Nat.Prime (p i) ∧ p i ∣ n + ↑i + 1

declarations.docstring:
Is there some absolute constant $C > 0$ such that
$$
  \sum_{p \leq n} 1_{p\nmid {2n \choose n}}\frac{1}{p} \leq C
$$
for all $n$?
references: [erdosproblems.com/377](https://www.erdosproblems.com/377)

declarations.docstring:
Erdos, Graham, Ruzsa, and Straus proved that if
$$
  f(n) = \sum_{p \leq n} 1_{p\nmid {2n \choose n}}\frac{1}{p}
$$
and
$$
  \gamma_0 = \sum_{k = 2}^{\infty} \frac{\log k}{2^k}
$$
then for almost all integers $f(m) = \gamma_0 + o(1)$, i.e. for every $\varepsilon > 0$ the set of
$n$ with $|f(n) - \gamma_0| < \varepsilon$ has natural density one.

[EGRS75] Erdős, P. and Graham, R. L. and Ruzsa, I. Z. and Straus, E. G., _On the prime factors of $\binom{2n}{n}$_. Math. Comp. (1975), 83-92.
references: [erdosproblems.com/377](https://www.erdosproblems.com/377)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (γ₀ : ℝ),
  γ₀ = ∑' (k : ℕ), Real.log (↑k + 2) / 2 ^ (k + 2) →
    ∀ ε > 0, {n | |Erdos377.sumInvPrimesNotDvdCentralBinom n - γ₀| < ε}.HasDensity 1

declarations.docstring:
Erdos, Graham, Ruzsa, and Straus proved that if
$$
  f(n) = \sum_{p \leq n} 1_{p\nmid {2n \choose n}}\frac{1}{p}
$$
and
$$
  \gamma_0 = \sum_{k = 2}^{\infty} \frac{\log k}{2^k}
$$
then
$$
  \lim_{x\to\infty} \frac{1}{x}\sum_{n\leq x} f(n) = \gamma_0
$$

[EGRS75] Erdős, P. and Graham, R. L. and Ruzsa, I. Z. and Straus, E. G., _On the prime factors of $\binom{2n}{n}$_. Math. Comp. (1975), 83-92.
references: [erdosproblems.com/377](https://www.erdosproblems.com/377)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (γ₀ : ℝ),
  γ₀ = ∑' (k : ℕ), Real.log (↑k + 2) / 2 ^ (k + 2) →
    Filter.Tendsto (fun x => 1 / ↑x * ∑ n ∈ Finset.Icc 1 x, Erdos377.sumInvPrimesNotDvdCentralBinom n) Filter.atTop
      (nhds γ₀)

declarations.docstring:
Erdos, Graham, Ruzsa, and Straus proved that if
$$
  f(n) = \sum_{p \leq n} 1_{p\nmid {2n \choose n}}\frac{1}{p}
$$
and
$$
  \gamma_0 = \sum_{k = 2}^{\infty} \frac{\log k}{2^k}
$$
then
$$
  \lim_{x\to\infty} \frac{1}{x}\sum_{n\leq x} f(n)^2 = \gamma_0^2
$$

$$
then there is some constant $c < 1$ such that for all large $n$
$$

$$

declarations.docstring:
Let $u \leq v$ be such that the largest prime dividing $\prod_{u \leq m \leq v} m$ appears with
exponent at least $2$. Is it true that $v - u = v^{o(1)}$?

We read this as: for every $\epsilon > 0$, every such pair with $v$ large enough satisfies
$v - u \leq v^{\epsilon}$. Cambie observed that this question reduces to old conjectures on gaps
between primes; for example, it follows from Cramér's conjecture. See also Erdős Problems 380 and
383.
references: [erdosproblems.com/382](https://www.erdosproblems.com/382)
[ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ ε > 0, ∀ᶠ (v : ℕ) in Filter.atTop, ∀ (u : ℕ), Erdos382.LargestPrimeRepeated u v → ↑(v - u) ≤ ↑v ^ ε

declarations.docstring:
Let $u \leq v$ be such that the largest prime dividing $\prod_{u \leq m \leq v} m$ appears with
exponent at least $2$. Can $v - u$ be arbitrarily large?

That is, for every $k$, is there such a pair with $v - u \geq k$? Cambie gives a heuristic that
suggests the answer is yes.
references: [erdosproblems.com/382](https://www.erdosproblems.com/382)
[ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (k : ℕ), ∃ u v, Erdos382.LargestPrimeRepeated u v ∧ k ≤ v - u

declarations.docstring:

$v - u \leq v^{1/2+o(1)}$ for every pair $u \leq v$ as in `Erdos382.erdos_382.parts.i`.

That is, for every $\epsilon > 0$, every such pair with $v$ large enough satisfies
$v - u \leq v^{1/2+\epsilon}$.
references: [erdosproblems.com/382](https://www.erdosproblems.com/382)
[ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ ε > 0, ∀ᶠ (v : ℕ) in Filter.atTop, ∀ (u : ℕ), Erdos382.LargestPrimeRepeated u v → ↑(v - u) ≤ ↑v ^ (1 / 2 + ε)

declarations.docstring:
The pair $(48, 50)$ satisfies the condition: $48 \cdot 49 \cdot 50 = 2^5 \cdot 3 \cdot 5^2
\cdot 7^2$, and the largest prime $7$ appears with exponent $2$.
references: [erdosproblems.com/382](https://www.erdosproblems.com/382)
[ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).

declarations.docstring:
If the condition holds, then $v < 2u$.

Otherwise $2u \leq v$, and by Bertrand's postulate there is a prime $q$ with $v/2 < q \leq v$, so
$u \leq q \leq v$. The largest prime $p$ of the product satisfies $p \geq q > v/2$. Hence $p$
divides exactly one factor $m \in [u, v]$, namely $m = p$, and $p$ appears with exponent $1$.
references: [erdosproblems.com/382](https://www.erdosproblems.com/382)
[ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ {u v : ℕ}, Erdos382.LargestPrimeRepeated u v → v < 2 * u

declarations.docstring:
Are there only finitely many solutions of
$$\prod_{1\leq i\leq k_1}(m_1+i)=\prod_{1\leq j\leq k_2}(m_2+j)$$
with $k_1,k_2>3$ and $m_1+k_1\leq m_2$?

Here $m_1, m_2 \geq 0$, so every factor is positive and the condition $m_1 + k_1 \leq m_2$ makes the
two blocks disjoint. Negative $m_1$ would give trivial solutions such as
$(-5)(-4)(-3)(-2) = 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 4 \cdot 5$. The source also asks to classify all solutions;
see `Erdos388.erdos_388.variants.classification`.
references: [erdosproblems.com/388](https://www.erdosproblems.com/388)

[Er76d] Erdős, P., *Problems and results on number theoretic properties of consecutive integers and related questions*. Proceedings of the Fifth Manitoba Conference on Numerical Mathematics (Univ. Manitoba, Winnipeg, Man., 1975) (1976), 25-44.
[ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
[Er92e] Erdős, Pál, *Some Unsolved problems in Geometry, Number Theory and Combinatorics*. Eureka (1992), 44-48.

{(m₁, k₁, m₂, k₂) |
    3 < k₁ ∧ 3 < k₂ ∧ m₁ + k₁ ≤ m₂ ∧ ∏ i ∈ Finset.Icc 1 k₁, (m₁ + i) = ∏ j ∈ Finset.Icc 1 k₂, (m₂ + j)}.Finite

with $k_1,k_2>3$ and $m_1+k_1\leq m_2$?

A solution must supply the set of all solutions $(m_1, k_1, m_2, k_2)$. Whether a description of
this set is a satisfactory classification is up to human judgement.
references: [erdosproblems.com/388](https://www.erdosproblems.com/388)

declarations.docstring:
More generally, if $k_1>2$ then for fixed $a$ and $b$ the equation
$$a\prod_{1\leq i\leq k_1}(m_1+i)=b\prod_{1\leq j\leq k_2}(m_2+j)$$
should have only finitely many solutions.

The source states no condition on $a$, $b$, $k_2$ or the position of the blocks, so this is our
reading: $a$ and $b$ are positive integers, we keep the condition $m_1+k_1\leq m_2$ of the main
problem (the $k_1$-block lies below the $k_2$-block), and we assume $k_2 > 2$ as well. Without
these conditions there are infinite families of solutions:
- for $k_2 = 1$ and $b = 1$, take $m_2 + 1 = a\prod_{1\leq i\leq k_1}(m_1+i)$;
- for $k_2 = 2$, $a = 1$ and $b = 4$, the identity $(n+1)(n+2)(n+3)(n+4) = Y(Y+2)$ with
  $Y = (n+1)(n+4)$ even gives a solution with $m_2 + 1 = Y/2$ for every $n \geq 2$;
- overlapping blocks give $2\prod_{1\leq i\leq k}(k-1+i)=\prod_{1\leq j\leq k}(k+j)$ for every
  $k \geq 2$.
references: [erdosproblems.com/388](https://www.erdosproblems.com/388)

[Er76d] Erdős, P., *Problems and results on number theoretic properties of consecutive integers and related questions*. Proceedings of the Fifth Manitoba Conference on Numerical Mathematics (Univ. Manitoba, Winnipeg, Man., 1975) (1976), 25-44.

[Er92e] Erdős, Pál, *Some Unsolved problems in Geometry, Number Theory and Combinatorics*. Eureka (1992), 44-48.

  0 < a →
    0 < b →

          2 < k₁ ∧
            2 < k₂ ∧ m₁ + k₁ ≤ m₂ ∧ a * ∏ i ∈ Finset.Icc 1 k₁, (m₁ + i) = b * ∏ j ∈ Finset.Icc 1 k₂, (m₂ + j)}.Finite

declarations.docstring:
Let $f(n)$ denote the minimal $m\geq 1$ such that
$$n! = a_1\cdots a_t$$
with $a_1<\cdots <a_t=a_1+m$. What is the behaviour of $f(n)$?

We formalise the question as: does $f(n) \to \infty$? A result of Luca [Lu02] implies a positive
answer, conditional on the $abc$ conjecture (see `Erdos393.erdos_393.variants.luca`).
references: [erdosproblems.com/393](https://www.erdosproblems.com/393)
[ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
[BeOs92] Berend, Daniel and Osgood, Charles F., *On the equation $P(x)=n!$ and a question of Erdős*. J. Number Theory 42 (1992), 189-193.

[Lu02] Luca, Florian, *The Diophantine equation $P(x)=n!$ and a result of M. Overholt*. Glas. Mat. Ser. III 37 (2002), 269-273.

declarations.docstring:
Let $F_m(N)$ count the number of $n \leq N$ such that $f(n) = m$. A theorem of Berend and
Osgood [BeOs92] implies that, for each fixed $m$, $F_m(N) = o(N)$, that is,
$\{n : f(n) = m\}$ has natural density $0$.

They proved that, for every $P \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ of degree at least $2$, the set of $n$ such
that $P(x) = n!$ has an integer solution has density $0$. For $m \geq 1$ this applies because
$f(n) = m$ gives $n! = P(a_1)$ for one of the finitely many polynomials
$P(x) = \prod_{j \in S} (x + j)$ with $\{0, m\} \subseteq S \subseteq \{0, \ldots, m\}$. For
$m = 0$ the set is $\{0, 1\}$ (the junk values), so the statement is trivial.
references: [erdosproblems.com/393](https://www.erdosproblems.com/393)
[ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
[BeOs92] Berend, Daniel and Osgood, Charles F., *On the equation $P(x)=n!$ and a question of Erdős*. J. Number Theory 42 (1992), 189-193.

[BPZ23] Bui, Hung M. and Pratt, Kyle and Zaharescu, Alexandru, *Power savings for counting solutions to polynomial-factorial equations*. Adv. Math. 422 (2023), Paper No. 109021, 32 pp. [arXiv:2204.08423](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.08423)
[Lu02] Luca, Florian, *The Diophantine equation $P(x)=n!$ and a result of M. Overholt*. Glas. Mat. Ser. III 37 (2002), 269-273.
[OEIS A388302](https://oeis.org/A388302): the values $f(n)$ for $n \geq 2$.
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (m : ℕ), {n | Erdos393.f n = m}.HasDensity 0

declarations.docstring:
A theorem of Bui, Pratt, and Zaharescu [BPZ23] implies that, for each fixed $m$,
$$F_m(N) \ll_m N^{33/34},$$
where $F_m(N)$ is the number of $n \leq N$ such that $f(n) = m$.

They proved that, for every $P \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ of degree at least $2$, the number of
$N \leq n < 2N$ such that $P(x) = n!$ has an integer solution is $\ll_P N^{33/34}$. Summing over
the finitely many polynomials in `Erdos393.erdos_393.variants.berend_osgood` and over the dyadic
ranges $[2^i, 2^{i+1})$ gives the bound for $n \leq N$.

$$\lvert A\cap \{1,\ldots,N\}\rvert \gg \frac{N^{1/2}}{g(N)}$$

declarations.docstring:
Let $\phi(n)$ be the Euler totient function and $\phi_k(n)$ be the iterated $\phi$ function, so
that $\phi_1(n)=\phi(n)$ and $\phi_k(n)=\phi(\phi_{k-1}(n))$. Let
$$f(n) = \min\{k : \phi_k(n)=1\}.$$
Does $f(n)/\log n$ have a distribution function?

We ask for a distribution function $F$ (non-decreasing, with $F(-\infty) = 0$ and
$F(+\infty) = 1$) such that, for every continuity point $c$ of $F$, the set
$\{n : f(n)/\log n \leq c\}$ has natural density $F(c)$. For $n \leq 1$ the quotient is $0$ in
Lean, which does not affect densities. Erdős, Granville, Pomerance and Spiro [EGPS90] proved
that the answer is yes, conditional on a form of the Elliott–Halberstam conjecture.
references: [erdosproblems.com/408](https://www.erdosproblems.com/408)
[OEIS A003434](https://oeis.org/A003434): the values $f(n)$ for $n \geq 2$.
[ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathématique (1980).

[Pi29] Pillai, S. Sivasankaranarayana, *On a function connected with $\phi(n)$*. Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. 35 (1929), 837-841. [doi:10.1090/S0002-9904-1929-04800-6](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0002-9904-1929-04800-6)
[Sh50] Shapiro, Harold N., *On the iterates of a certain class of arithmetic functions*. Comm. Pure Appl. Math. 3 (1950), 259-272.

[EGPS90] Erdős, P., Granville, A., Pomerance, C. and Spiro, C., *On the normal behavior of the iterates of some arithmetic functions*. Analytic number theory (Allerton Park, IL, 1989), Progr. Math. 85 (1990), 165-204.
[Gu04] Guy, Richard K., *Unsolved problems in number theory*. Third edition, Springer (2004), Problem B41.

[FKL10] Ford, K., Konyagin, S. V. and Luca, F., *Prime chains and Pratt trees*. Geom. Funct. Anal. 20 (2010), 1231-1258. [arXiv:0904.0473](https://arxiv.org/abs/0904.0473) [doi:10.1007/s00039-010-0089-0](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00039-010-0089-0)
declarations.type_pretty:
∃ F,
  Monotone F ∧
    Filter.Tendsto F Filter.atBot (nhds 0) ∧
      Filter.Tendsto F Filter.atTop (nhds 1) ∧
        ∀ (c : ℝ), ContinuousAt F c → {n | ↑(Erdos408.f n) / Real.log ↑n ≤ c}.HasDensity (F c)

declarations.docstring:
Is $f(n)/\log n$ almost always constant?

We read this as: is there a constant $\alpha$ such that, for every $\epsilon > 0$, the set of
$n$ with $|f(n)/\log n - \alpha| < \epsilon$ has natural density $1$? Erdős, Granville,
Pomerance and Spiro [EGPS90] proved that, conditional on a form of the Elliott–Halberstam
conjecture, $f(n)$ has normal order $\alpha \log n$ for some constant $\alpha > 0$, so that the
answer is yes under this hypothesis.
references: [erdosproblems.com/408](https://www.erdosproblems.com/408)
[OEIS A003434](https://oeis.org/A003434): the values $f(n)$ for $n \geq 2$.
[ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathématique (1980).

declarations.docstring:
The third question asks what can be said about the largest prime factor $P^+(\phi_k(n))$ when,
say, $k = \log\log n$; it is open-ended and is not formalised. The site remarks that it is likely
true that, if $k \to \infty$ however slowly with $n$, then $P^+(\phi_k(n)) \leq n^{o(1)}$ for
almost all $n$.

Ford, Konyagin and Luca [FKL10, Theorem 5] proved that for every $\epsilon > 0$ and $\delta > 0$
there is an integer $k$ such that, for all large $x$, at least $(1 - \epsilon)x$ integers
$n \leq x$ satisfy $P^+(\phi_k(n)) \leq x^{\delta}$. Since $P^+(\phi(m)) \leq P^+(m)$, this gives
the remark above for every $k = k(n) \to \infty$.

declarations.docstring:
Pillai [Pi29] proved that, for all $n \geq 2$,
$$\left\lfloor \frac{\log n - \log 2}{\log 3} \right\rfloor + 1 \leq f(n) \leq
  \left\lfloor \frac{\log n}{\log 2} \right\rfloor + 1.$$
These are Theorems I and III of [Pi29]; Pillai's function $R(n)$ is the least $r$ with
$\phi_r(n) = 1$, which is $f(n)$. The lower bound is attained at $n = 2 \cdot 3^k$, and
$f(2^k) = k$ (`Erdos408.f_two_pow`), so the upper bound cannot be replaced by $f(n) < \log_2 n$.

declarations.docstring:
Erdős proved that the barrier set for `expProd` is infinite and even has positive density.

`HasPosDensity` is the right reading rather than positive lower density. In [Er79d] this is
Theorem 1, "the density of integers satisfying (2) is positive", where `d₀(n) = ∏ αᵢ` is
`expProd`. The averaging argument there bounds the density below, but Erdős states the existence
separately on the last page: "With a little more trouble, I can prove that the density of
integers `n` for which `n` is a barrier for `d₀(n)` exists." He goes further, that if `αᵢ` is the
density of `n` with `max_{m<n} (m + d₀(m)) = n + i`, then every `αᵢ` exists and they sum to `1`.

[Er79d] Erdős, P., *Some unconventional problems in number theory*.
Acta Math. Acad. Sci. Hungar. (1979), 71-80.
references: [erdosproblems.com/413](https://www.erdosproblems.com/413)
[A5236](https://oeis.org/A5236)
declarations.type_pretty: {n | Erdos413.IsBarrier (fun m => ↑(Erdos413.expProd m)) n}.HasPosDensity

declarations.docstring:
Are there infinitely many integers not of the form $n - \phi(n)$?

Asked by Erdős and Sierpiński. Numbers not of the form we call non-cototients.

Browkin and Schinzel [BrSc95] provided an affirmative answer to this question, proving that any
integer of the shape $2^{k}\cdot 509203$ for $k\geq 1$ is a non-cototient.

This is discussed in problem B36 of Guy's collection [Gu04].

This was formalized in Lean by Alexeev using Aristotle.
references: [erdosproblems.com/418](https://www.erdosproblems.com/418)
[Wikipedia: Noncototient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noncototient)

declarations.docstring:
It follows from a slight strengthening of the Goldbach conjecture that every odd number can be
written as $n - \phi(n)$.
In particular, we assume that every even number greater than 6 can be written as the sum of two
*distinct* primes, in contrast to the usual Goldbach conjecture that every even number greater than
2 can be written as the sum of two primes.

The **Odd Noncototient Conjecture**: every non-cototient is even. Equivalently, every odd natural
number is of the form $n - \phi(n)$ for some $n$.

This is the unconditional form of `erdos_418.variants.conditional`, which derives the odd case from a
strengthening of the Goldbach conjecture. See [Wikipedia: Noncototient].

declarations.docstring:
Erdős [Er73b] has shown that a positive density set of natural numbers cannot be written as
$\sigma(n)-n$ (numbers not of this form are called nonaliquot, or sometimes untouchable).

Here "positive density" means positive lower density: Banks and Luca [BaLu05] proved that the
set of nonaliquots has lower density at least $1/48$, Chen and Zhao [ChZh11] improved this to
$0.06$, and it is not known whether the natural density of the nonaliquots exists (Pollack and
Pomerance [PoPo16] give a heuristic predicting its value).

declarations.docstring:
If $\tau(n)$ counts the number of divisors of $n$ then let
$$F(f,n)=\frac{\tau((n+\lfloor f(n)\rfloor)!)}{\tau(n!)}.$$
Is it true that
$$\lim_{n\to \infty}F((\log n)^C,n)=\infty$$
for large $C$?

"For large $C$" means for all sufficiently large real $C$. Since $(\log n)^C$ increases with $C$
for $n \geq 3$ and $F(f,n)$ is nondecreasing in $f(n)$, this is equivalent to asking for one
such $C$.
references: [erdosproblems.com/420](https://www.erdosproblems.com/420)

declarations.type_pretty: ∀ᶠ (C : ℝ) in Filter.atTop, Filter.Tendsto (Erdos420.F fun m => Real.log ↑m ^ C) Filter.atTop Filter.atTop

declarations.docstring:
Is it true that $F(\log n,n)$ is everywhere dense in $(1,\infty)$?

This asks that every point of $(1,\infty)$ lies in the closure of the set of values
$F(\log n, n)$. Note that $F(f,n) \geq 1$ always (`Erdos420.one_le_F`).

$n\to \infty$, then is $F(f,n)$ everywhere dense?

declarations.docstring:
Let $a_1 = 2$ and $a_2 = 3$ and continue the sequence by appending to $a_1, \ldots, a_n$ all possible
values of $a_i a_j - 1$ with $i \neq j$.
Is it true that the set of integers which eventually appear has positive density?

As explained on [erdosproblems.com/424](https://www.erdosproblems.com/424), "positive density"
here means positive *lower* density: is there $c > 0$ such that for all large $x$ at least
$cx$ of the integers in $[1, x]$ appear? See `erdos_424.variants.exact_density` for the
literal reading.

The answer is yes: Korsky [Ko26] (with ChatGPT 5.6 Pro) proved that the set has positive lower
density. The linked formal proof (Alexeev and Codex) shows that there is `c > 0` with
`c * x ≤ #{n ∈ [1, x] | n ∈ generatedSet}` for all large `x`, which gives
`c / 2 ≤ generatedSet.lowerDensity`.
references: [erdosproblems.com/424](https://www.erdosproblems.com/424)
[A5244](https://oeis.org/A5244)
[Ben Green's Open Problem 63](https://people.maths.ox.ac.uk/greenbj/papers/open-problems.pdf#section.8 Problem 63)
[Ko26] Korsky, S., *A problem of Erdős on the sequence $a_ia_j - 1$*, [arXiv:2608.07910](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07910)
declarations.type_pretty: 0 < Erdos424.generatedSet.lowerDensity

declarations.docstring:
Let $F(n)$ be the maximum size of a subset of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ with distinct
pairwise products. Is there a constant $c > 0$ such that
$$F(n) = \pi(n) + (c + o(1)) n^{3/4}(\log n)^{-3/2}?$$
references: [Erdős Problem 425](https://www.erdosproblems.com/425)
declarations.type_pretty:
∃ c,
  0 < c ∧
    Filter.Tendsto
      (fun n => (↑(Erdos425.pairProductExtremal n) - ↑n.primeCounting) / (↑n ^ (3 / 4) * Real.log ↑n ^ (-3 / 2)))
      Filter.atTop (nhds c)

declarations.docstring:
If all products of $r$ distinct elements of $A \subseteq \{1,\ldots,n\}$ are
distinct, must
$$|A| \leq \pi(n) + O\bigl(n^{(r+1)/(2r)}\bigr)?$$
references: [Erdős Problem 425](https://www.erdosproblems.com/425)
declarations.type_pretty:
∀ (r : ℕ),
  1 ≤ r →
    ∃ C,
      0 < C ∧
        ∀ᶠ (n : ℕ) in Filter.atTop,
          ∀ A ⊆ Finset.Icc 1 n,
            Erdos425.RProductsDistinct r A → ↑A.card ≤ ↑n.primeCounting + C * ↑n ^ ((↑r + 1) / (2 * ↑r))

declarations.docstring: Products of two distinct elements are distinct exactly when pairwise products are.
references: [Erdős Problem 425](https://www.erdosproblems.com/425)

declarations.docstring:
Is there a set $A\subseteq \mathbb{N}$ such that, for infinitely many $n$, all of $n-a$
are prime for all $a\in A$ with $0 < a < n$ and $$\liminf\frac{\lvert A\cap [1,x]\rvert}{\pi(x)}>0?$$
references: [erdosproblems.com/428](https://www.erdosproblems.com/428)

True ↔
  ∃ A,
    (∃ᶠ (n : ℕ) in Filter.atTop, ∀ a ∈ A, 0 < a → a < n → Nat.Prime (n - a)) ∧
      Filter.liminf (fun n => Erdos428.primeDensityRatio A n) Filter.atTop > 0

declarations.docstring:
Fix some integer $n$ and define a decreasing sequence in $[1,n)$ by $a_1=n-1$ and, for
$k\geq 2$, letting $a_k$ be the greatest integer in $[1,a_{k-1})$ such that all of the prime
factors of $a_k$ are $>n-a_k$.

Is it true that, for sufficiently large $n$, not all of this sequence can be prime?
references: [erdosproblems.com/430](https://www.erdosproblems.com/430)
[ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).

declarations.docstring:
If $p$ is a prime and $k, m \geq 2$, let $r(k, m, p)$ be the minimal $r$ such that
$r, r + 1, \ldots, r + m - 1$ are all $k$th power residues modulo $p$, and let
$\Lambda(k, m) = \limsup_{p \to \infty} r(k, m, p)$. Is $\Lambda(k, 2)$ finite for all $k$?

A question of Lehmer and Lehmer [LeLe62]. Hildebrand [Hi91] proved that $\Lambda(k, 2)$ is finite
for all $k \geq 2$.
references: [erdosproblems.com/436](https://www.erdosproblems.com/436)

declarations.docstring:
**Erdős Problem 44:** Let N ≥ 1 and `A ⊆ {1,…,N}` be a Sidon set. Is it true that, for any ε > 0,
there exist M = M(ε) and `B ⊆ {N+1,…,M}` such that `A ∪ B ⊆ {1,…,M}` is a Sidon set
of size at least `(1−ε)M^{1/2}`?

This problem asks whether any Sidon set can be extended to achieve a density
arbitrarily close to the optimal density for Sidon sets.
references: [erdosproblems.com/44](https://www.erdosproblems.com/44)
declarations.type_pretty:
True ↔
  ∀ N ≥ 1,
    ∀ A ⊆ Finset.Icc 1 N,
      IsSidon ↑A → ∀ ε > 0, ∃ M > N, ∃ B ⊆ Finset.Icc (N + 1) M, IsSidon (↑A ∪ ↑B) ∧ (1 - ε) * √↑M ≤ ↑(A ∪ B).card

declarations.docstring: The case where we start with an empty set (constructing large Sidon sets).
references: [erdosproblems.com/44](https://www.erdosproblems.com/44)
declarations.type_pretty: True ↔ ∀ ε > 0, ∀ᶠ (M : ℕ) in Filter.atTop, ∃ A ⊆ Finset.Icc 1 M, IsSidon ↑A ∧ (1 - ε) * √↑M ≤ ↑A.card

declarations.docstring: The set `{1, 2, 4, 8, 13}` is a Sidon set in `{1, ..., 13}`.
references: [erdosproblems.com/44](https://www.erdosproblems.com/44)

declarations.docstring: The greedy construction gives a Sidon set of size approximately `√N`.
references: [erdosproblems.com/44](https://www.erdosproblems.com/44)
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (N : ℕ), 1 ≤ N → ∃ A ⊆ Finset.Icc 1 N, IsSidon ↑A ∧ A.card ≥ N.sqrt

declarations.docstring: The maximum size of a Sidon set in `{1, ..., N}` is less than or equal to `2 * √N`.
references: [erdosproblems.com/44](https://www.erdosproblems.com/44)
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (N : ℕ), 1 ≤ N → ↑(Finset.Icc 1 N).maxSidonSubsetCard ≤ 2 * √↑N

declarations.docstring: For any `N`, there exists a Sidon set of size at least `√N/2`.
references: [erdosproblems.com/44](https://www.erdosproblems.com/44)
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (N : ℕ), 1 ≤ N → ∃ A ⊆ Finset.Icc 1 N, IsSidon ↑A ∧ N.sqrt / 2 ≤ A.card

declarations.docstring:
Is it true that, for any $c>1/2$, if $p$ is a sufficiently large prime then, for any
$n\geq 0$, there exist $a,b\in(n,n+p^c)$ such that $ab\equiv 1\pmod{p}$?

This is discussed in this MathOverflow question [MathOverflow].
references: [erdosproblems.com/445](https://www.erdosproblems.com/445)
[He00] Heath-Brown, D. R., Arithmetic applications of {K}loosterman sums. Nieuw Arch. Wiskd. (5) (2000), 380--384.
[MathOverflow](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/69509/small-residue-classes-with-small-reciprocal)
declarations.type_pretty: True ↔ ∀ c > 1 / 2, ∀ᶠ (p : ℕ) in Filter.atTop, Nat.Prime p → ∀ (n : ℕ), Erdos445.Erdos445Prop c p n

declarations.docstring:
Small example: for $p=5$, $c=1$, $n=0$, the pair $(2,3) \in (0,5)$ satisfies
$2 \cdot 3 = 6 \equiv 1 \pmod{5}$.
references: [erdosproblems.com/445](https://www.erdosproblems.com/445)
[He00] Heath-Brown, D. R., Arithmetic applications of {K}loosterman sums. Nieuw Arch. Wiskd. (5) (2000), 380--384.
[MathOverflow](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/69509/small-residue-classes-with-small-reciprocal)
declarations.type_pretty: Erdos445.Erdos445Prop 1 5 1

declarations.docstring:
How large must $y=y(\epsilon,n)$ be such that the number of integers in
$(x,x+y)$ with a divisor in $(n,2n)$ is at most $\epsilon y$?

The bound is required for every $x$ and every window length at least $y$, and
$y(\epsilon,n)$ is the least such threshold (or $\infty$ if there is none).
A **linear** scale $y \le C(\epsilon) n$ is known to suffice for fixed $\epsilon$
and all large $n$ (see `erdos_450.linear_scale_suffices`).
references: [erdosproblems.com/450](https://www.erdosproblems.com/450)
declarations.type_pretty: ∀ (ε : ℝ), 0 < ε → ∀ (n : ℕ), Erdos450.windowThreshold ε n = Erdos450.erdos_450.answer

declarations.docstring:
A translate-uniform **linear** scale suffices: there is a sufficient window
length `Y` with `Y ε n ≤ C(ε) · n`. This is an upper bound on the optimal scale,
not the exact threshold asked for in `erdos_450`.
references: [erdosproblems.com/450](https://www.erdosproblems.com/450)
declarations.type_pretty: ∃ Y, (∀ (ε : ℝ), 0 < ε → ∃ C, ∀ (n : ℕ), ↑(Y ε n) ≤ C * ↑n) ∧ Erdos450.IsSufficientScale Y
